key_insight: Early three-dimensional vorticity evolution in transonic shock–boundary-layer interactions is dominated by viscous and compressibility-related mechanisms, with vortex stretching becoming appreciable but intermittent during shock-induced separation.
engineering_relevance: Understanding when three-dimensional effects emerge can inform the use of two-dimensional simulations to assess natural-laminar-flow airfoil performance near transonic operating limits.
method: High-fidelity 3D simulations of the SHM1 airfoil across normal-shock development, drag divergence, and shock-induced separation.
Comparison of spanwise-averaged 3D surface pressure and skin friction with previously reported 2D simulations.
Streamwise and wall-normal enstrophy tracking and compressible enstrophy-transport budget analysis.
evidence_signal: Across three operating conditions, 2D–3D comparisons identify an initial agreement interval and subsequent departures, while normalized enstrophy budgets show regime-dependent redistribution among the same principal mechanisms.
watch_item: The study addresses short-time evolution on one airfoil; its findings do not establish long-time behavior or universal limits for 2D modeling.
paper_title: Onset of three dimensionality in transonic shock boundary layer interaction over a natural laminar flow airfoil
